speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I also note that Mr Zaqy Mohamad had asked a related Parliamentary Question (PQ) scheduled for this range of Sittings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Whether it is an attack by a radicalised Muslim individual, or an attack by an extremist Islamophobe − which happened in London a few weeks ago − all these are terror attacks which have no place in our society or any society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As seen in the UK, terror attacks can take place anywhere, anytime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: How do we completely guard against someone who decides to drive a car into a crowded public area?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Or someone who goes on a stabbing rampage with a kitchen knife?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These are very difficult security challenges, which we and our counterparts around the world take very seriously.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Zaqy Mohamad asked about this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In evaluating the various options, we will take into account several factors, including: (a) function, in short, how effective will the measures be in addressing the threat; (b) form, how the measures will fit into the surroundings and be part of the surroundings; and (c) impact on users, will the measures significantly restrict day-to-day usage of the space.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We could try and fortify the entire city.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But this is not a sensible or practical approach.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will have to strike a balance between enhancing security which is very important, on the one hand, and the possibility of disrupting day-to-day activities through the imposition of curbs and restrictions, which will inconvenience users, on the other hand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These security measures will also come at a significant cost to taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Government will need to make a practical assessment about the type and extent of measures we put in place to enhance security for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These measures will complement the laws and stakeholder engagement processes that we already have or will be implementing in the coming months.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We amended the Public Order Act in April this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to work with public and private sector stakeholders to enhance the security of buildings and public spaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: An updated version of the Guidelines for Enhancing Building Security in Singapore will be released later this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Specific to schools, as Miss Cheng Li Hui had asked, MHA works closely with MOE.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We keep MOE informed of the overall security threat climate and risks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Based on this, MOE works with us to review and calibrate the security measures for schools.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is important to put in place laws and other security measures to prevent an attack.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I now want to focus on the second threat of radicalisation and extremism which is the threat to our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is less apparent than any immediate loss of life, but can be greatly damaging to our nation as a whole.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Minister for Home Affairs has spoken at length on various occasions about this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Today, I will speak on two specific groups which Miss Cheng Li Hui and Mr Christopher de Souza asked about: (a) students and school staff; and (b) foreigners.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Most of the Singaporeans who have been radicalised were younger than 30.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our youths consume a lot of information from the Internet and social media.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They exploit these media to spread their radical ideologies and terrorist propaganda.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our youth spend a significant proportion of their time in schools and educational institutions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Schools are, therefore, key platforms for us to counter these dangerous influences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Through Social Studies and Character & Citizenship Education lessons, MOE inculcates in our students values of living harmoniously in Singapore's multi-racial and multi-religious society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MHA has also worked with MOE to incorporate counter-terrorism messages into the Secondary school curriculum.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our schools provide a supportive environment for our students to build strong, positive relationships with their peers and teachers from different races and religions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These social bonds are the strongest counter against any exclusivist or extremist mindset.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Teachers and counsellors also look out for students who display anti-social behaviour.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We do our best to intervene and provide guidance early to prevent such behaviour from spiralling into more dangerous forms of extremism.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MHA conducts workshops for teachers and counsellors to sensitise them to the heightened threat environment, as well as increase their understanding of terrorist ideologies and tell-tale signs of radicalisation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They play an important role in identifying students or co-workers who may be radicalised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Even as we put in all these measures, the responsibility of inoculating our young from radical, extremist influences cannot be left to schools alone.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Family members, friends, colleagues, religious leaders and community leaders play an important role.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will come back to this later in my reply.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked for an update on the threat by radicalised foreigners in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We updated the House on seven cases in January this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Since then, another two more have been detected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Similar to the earlier cases, both of them were ISIS supporters, radicalised through social media.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One of them intended to travel to Syria with her foreign boyfriend to join ISIS.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: None of the nine had plans to carry out acts of violence in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we cannot condone support for any radical ideologies in Singapore − whether by locals or foreigners.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MHA has worked closely with MOM to address the threat of radicalised foreigner workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: After the arrest of the radicalised Bangladeshi nationals last year, we prepared an advisory for foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We advised them to be alert, watch out for signs of radicalisation among their co-workers and to report any possible radicalisation to the authorities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will do more, to sensitise our foreign workers to Singapore's multi-religious social values.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will take place throughout their time working in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Upon arrival in Singapore, all foreign workers are required to visit the MOM Services Centre.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Education Gallery in the Centre will display messages that reinforce the dangers of radical ideologies, the need to be vigilant and to report any suspicious activities or radicalised workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: FDWs will be required to go through a Settling-In Programme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They will be sensitised to the threat of radicalisation and made aware that any form of radicalisation will not be condoned in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In their dormitories, foreign workers will be regularly engaged by agencies, such as MOM, the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS) and the Religious Rehabilitation Group (RRG).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They will be advised to call the RRG hotline should they require any advice − for themselves or with regard to someone they know.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MUIS is also looking to better manage the religious needs of Muslim foreign workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Foreigners are encouraged to seek religious advice only from ARS-accredited asatizah.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They can attend religious classes at our mosques and will continue to be welcomed and included in activities in the mosques and the broader community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will strengthen their understanding and appreciation of Singapore's multi-religious social values and norms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng asked if the current initiatives are sufficient.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui and Mr Christopher de Souza asked if more can be done.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Police have received many reports from members of the public on suspicious circumstances, from 999 calls and also via the SGSecure app.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The public is paying closer attention to our surroundings and does not hesitate to make reports to the authorities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The public's response to incidents, such as the closures of Hougang and Woodleigh MRT stations in April 2017, was also encouraging.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The large majority of Singaporeans understood the potential security threats and accepted the inconvenience caused as a result.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MHA will continue to work towards strengthening community vigilance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, SGSecure is not just about preventing a terrorist attack.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: More than that, it is about how we stand united as one Singapore, to help one another, after an attack.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the root of this is how we strengthen and safeguard our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MHA will continue to work with agencies like MCCY and the People's Association to implement community programmes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, MCCY is establishing the SGSecure Community Network to strengthen partnerships with religious and community organisations, to build greater mutual trust and understanding.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The community plays a critical role in strengthening and safeguarding our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, the role of family members in safeguarding against radicalisation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have made this point previously and repeatedly, but it is critical.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We talked about the risk of online radicalisation among our youths earlier in the reply.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Family members and friends are in the best position to notice signs of radicalisation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If an individual is spending excessive amounts of time on the Internet looking at suspicious, potentially radical material; or talks in praise of terrorist groups or about going overseas to take part in armed violence − family members and friends should alert the authorities immediately.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is a very difficult decision for any father, mother, brother or sister to make.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, this must be infinitely better than losing a son or daughter, brother or sister forever, to armed violence overseas or a suicide attack.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, the role of religious leaders and community leaders in encouraging community integration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NCCS recognised the contributions of the Muslim community to Singapore's progress and the strength of our multi-religious community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It made clear its position that the detention must not be used to stoke the flames of Islamophobia in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It can be as simple as a visit to a nearby place of worship of another religion to understand them, or sharing a meal with groups from other faiths.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, the role of the individual in building stronger friendships with those of a different race or religion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These are the foundations of our social fabric which have brought us to where we are today and we must protect them at all cost.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Minister had said recently that there were two more individuals picked up for radicalisation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can the Minister kindly share the profiles, if at all possible, of these two that were recently picked up?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My second question is, if it is a Singaporean who is being potentially radicalised, there is a family in Singapore and there is a family support network who could encourage him and even report him to get help.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My question is: is that not a little bit more difficult where it is a foreigner where he does not have that sort of accountability, mechanism, in the form of a family?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is MHA's approach to ensure that his peer support mechanism does report him?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: She wanted to travel, as I said, to Syria with a foreign boyfriend to join ISIS.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: She had worked in Singapore for two years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Member has also asked a question about how support networks can be created for foreign workers who come to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: During Ramadan, I visited a foreign dormitory, broke fast together with the management of the dormitory and the bosses of companies whose workers were housed in the dormitory.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I had some time to talk to some of the workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some have been here for many, many years; some had just arrived.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Those who had just arrived, I asked them, they said they had no friends yet but were actively trying to look out for people from their community back home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some would find, perhaps, relatives, both close or distant, friends from the same city or village, but some are just meeting people for the first time from the place where they come from.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, our foreign workers coming here to Singapore will try to build their networks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When you speak to some of the older foreign workers, those who have been here for a longer time, they say, "I look out for my younger brother.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If he is a new person, I will share with him." They are very conversant in English and are very familiar with our surroundings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I have spoken earlier in my response about the different things that agencies are doing to familiarise foreign workers before they even leave their home countries; when they arrive in Singapore, at different touchpoints in time, engaging RRG, MUIS and MOM to reach out to the foreign workers, talking to bosses of companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But when we sensitise the broader foreign worker community in Singapore to Singapore's multi-racial and multi-religious fabric, and about the importance of integration, many of them begin to be familiar with what to look out for.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is our hope that these will provide those informal social networks that the Member talked about.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They are like family to each other in their own way.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I have two supplementary questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We note that the recent attacks in London involved terrorists driving a truck and ramming into pedestrians along a pedestrian crossing.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Similar attacks could also happen in Orchard Road, which can be quite scary.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: While some say that it is healthy to see a crowd crossing a pedestrian crossing, it is also posing a threat.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: So, would MHA consider taking the lead in a whole-of-Government approach to encourage building owners to build linkages on the second level, overhead, or underground, to reduce such threats, rather than having the existing building regulations to compel the building owners to only build linkages during major renovations?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The second question is: will MHA consider increasing the number and scale of exercises in the heartlands involving the residents, so that they can be better prepared for the aftermath of an attack, if any?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I have said earlier, MHA is working with built environment agencies and relevant associations to look at what sensibly needs to be done to strengthen safety and security in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members would know that our security layers are multi-pronged, both outside Singapore and our borders and within Singapore − the law enforcement and security forces' responses and capabilities, but also individuals' responsibility – being alert, being aware what to do.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And being stakeholders in the community, building owners are also playing a part.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When Members talk about risks at road crossings, I think  if we put our mind to it, we can think of many, many other areas where we are soft targets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, if we cross an underground tunnel or overhead link, that, again, funnels crowds and gives rise to threats, maybe not vehicles, maybe knife threats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, the question is, do we want to harden the whole country?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Sometimes, we get suggestions that we should harden every area and screen at every possible place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have to strike the right balance because, pushed to the extreme, without an attack even occurring, terrorists would have won, if life in Singapore and any other city freezes up because of all these measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will, of course, come with lots of concerns between communities about each other.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, it is not just the infrastructure causing inconvenience and frustration, but also the whole sense of fear, a climate of fear, with regard to terrorism.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will look at all sensible measures that we need to put in place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But, again, we have to strike a balance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some people suggested we should do screening before crowds enter MRT stations or before they even enter an airport or a train station.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And then, someone pointed out, if you do that, you need to harden the queue outside the security screening point.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think we have to strike a balance and ensure that all layers, all stakeholders, take part.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Member's second question is about exercises in the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Member may be aware that we have revamped the Emergency Preparedness (EP) Day.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These revamped EP Days are one or two or three a month.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we are happy to work with stakeholders and with community partners who wish to join us in this joint fight against terrorism.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Minister, how is the Government responding to the on-going crisis in Marawi in the Philippines, something which has taken many in Southeast Asia by surprise?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Has the Ministry's perception of the threat to Singapore from terrorism changed as a result of it?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we also talked about the concern with regard to the south of the Philippines, with the ISIS' intention to set up a caliphate province.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That being very close to Singapore and our region, certainly raises security concerns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, MHA, together with other agencies, is actively looking at developments there and will make sure that the necessary security measures are in place.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Earlier, the Minister shared some of the profiles of those who have been radicalised.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Has MHA studied some of these profiles and seen a trend − who are these in the groups that are more vulnerable to radicalisation − so that that could, at least, enable us to target some of these segments?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My question is: what are some of these segments that are more vulnerable and has MHA profiled them?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The second question is: I understand there are also sites that they probably go to because a lot of the threats the Minister mentioned were online.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, does MHA also actively track these sites and what are we doing to block them or reduce access to these sites?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The third question relates to my Parliamentary Question No 39 which the Minister alluded to earlier − whether in constituencies or on the ground where the constituencies require or find that these are potential threats and we need to set up bollards and so forth, will items like these be put into schemes like the CIPC, for example, to be funded so that it would give constituencies or heartlands the autonomy to also set up some of these bollards where required?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Beyond that, operationally, I would not want to comment further on the questions the Member has raised, but MHA is actively keeping a look-out for radicalised individuals in Singapore, whether local or foreign.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In terms of sites, the Member asked whether we track or block sites.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As for bollards and other security measures that could reduce certain kinds of risk patterns, these are things that I have said earlier that MHA is actively working with the built environment agencies to look at.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are looking at various measures which we are not ready to announce at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But, at its base, we encourage heavy vehicle owners and car rental companies to be very mindful of the people that they rent their vehicles out to.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And car rental companies already are required to keep a register which will, again, allow them to filter threats.
